title: Reflexives and possessives: se, suus

objectives.can: Read se and suus as referring to the subject, and tell suus from eius.

explanation.summary: Latin has a reflexive pronoun (*se*, *sibi*) and a reflexive possessive (*suus*) that look back to the subject of their clause. They are different from *eius* and *eorum*, which name someone else. The possessives *meus*, *tuus*, *noster*, *vester* are ordinary adjectives that agree with the thing owned.

sections.heading: se: the pronoun that refers back to the subject
body: The reflexive pronoun has no nominative. Its forms are *se* (accusative and ablative), *sibi* (dative) and *sui* (genitive), and they are the same in the singular and the plural; the library files them under the headword *sui*. Because they refer back to the subject, they mean 'himself, herself, itself, themselves' (or 'for himself' and so on).

In *Et bajulans sibi crucem*, the dative *sibi* refers to the man who carries: 'carrying for himself his cross'. In *Qui dicit se in ipso manere*, the *se* refers to *qui*, the subject of *dicit*: 'he who says that he himself abides in him'. A reflexive in a reported statement usually refers to the speaker or thinker, the subject of the verb of saying.

In the analysed texts the form *se* is almost always left undecided between accusative and ablative, and *sese* likewise, so the generated questions mostly use *sibi*, which is certain. When you meet *se*, the clause decides: it is accusative as an object or in an accusative-and-infinitive, and ablative after a preposition such as *a* or *cum* when the preposition takes the ablative.

sections.heading: suus: 'his own', 'her own', 'their own'
body: *suus* is the possessive that goes with *se*. It is an adjective of the first and second declension: it agrees with the thing owned in case, number and gender, and it refers to the subject of its clause. In *Filium suum*, 'his own Son', *suum* is accusative singular masculine because it goes with *Filium*, and it refers to *Deus*, the subject. The word is the same whether the owner is one person or many.

sections.heading: suus or eius?
body: Classical Latin keeps the two apart. *suus* means 'his own' of the subject. *eius* means 'his' (or 'her') of someone other than the subject; *eorum* and *earum* mean 'their' of others. Compare the single verse Matthew 27:35: *diviserunt vestimenta ejus*, 'they divided his garments', where the garments are not the soldiers' but the crucified man's, and the quotation that follows, *diviserunt sibi vestimenta mea*, 'they divided my garments among themselves', where *sibi* refers back to the soldiers, who are the subject.

In Matthew 1:21, *populum suum a peccatis eorum* has both: 'his own people' (*suum*, referring to the subject *ipse*) and 'their sins' (*eorum*, the people's). The people are not the subject, so *eorum* is the right word.

The Vulgate is not strict. Under the influence of Greek, which has no reflexive possessive of this kind, the translator sometimes writes *eius* where a classical author would write *suus*. In Acts 16:15 the household (*domus ejus*) is that of the woman who is the subject of the sentence, and a classical writer would probably have *sua*. Read the sentence, not the rule: ask whose the thing is.

sections.heading: meus, tuus, noster, vester
body: The other four possessives are adjectives, and they agree with the thing owned, never with the owner. In *Meus cibus est*, 'my food is', *Meus* is nominative singular masculine because *cibus* is, and the speaker's own gender does not matter. In *vocationem vestram*, *vestram* is accusative singular feminine like *vocationem*; the people addressed are 'brothers', masculine, but the adjective does not follow them.
*meus* has a vocative singular *mi* in the masculine, and *noster* and *vester* lose the e in the oblique cases (*nostram*, *vestram*), as *ager* does (compare *agrum*).

misunderstandings: *suus* does not mean 'his' in the way English 'his' does. It means 'his own, her own, their own' and refers to the subject of the clause. For someone else's, the Latin uses *eius* or *eorum*.
A possessive does not agree with the owner. *Pater meus* is masculine because *Pater* is, not because the speaker is.
*se* is not the same as *me* or *te*. It stands for the third person only, and it is the same in the singular and the plural.
The rule that *suus* refers to the subject is a classical rule. In the Vulgate and the Fathers, *eius* can stand where *suus* would be expected, and the reverse also happens, so check the sentence.

deeper.heading: Reflexives in subordinate clauses
body: In a subordinate clause that reports someone's words or thoughts, *se* and *suus* usually refer to the person whose words or thoughts are reported, not to the subject of the nearest verb. This is the 'indirect reflexive'. It can make a sentence ambiguous, and Latin writers sometimes use *ipse* to settle which person is meant. Allen and Greenough describe the usual patterns; later Latin follows them less closely.

examples.analysis: *sibi* is the dative of the reflexive pronoun (headword *sui*). It refers to the subject of the sentence, the man who goes out, and means 'for himself': 'carrying his own cross'. The accusative *crucem* is what he carries.

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.english: And after they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots; that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet, saying: They divided my garments among them; and upon my vesture they cast lots.
quoted.credit: GoLearn Latin analyser (adapter-la; Whitaker's Words, Lewis & Short, Perseus treebank form priors, hand-written Vulgate priors); no Latinist has checked its data

examples.analysis: Two different words for the owner in one verse. *ejus* is not reflexive: the garments are those of the man they crucified, who is not the subject. *sibi* in the quotation refers to the subject, the soldiers: 'among themselves'. Whose garments? Look for the subject and ask whether the owner is the same person.

examples.analysis: *ejus* (the child's name) and *eorum* (the people's sins) are genitives of *is*. They name someone other than the subject of the sentence. In the same verse *suum* in *populum suum* refers to the subject *ipse*, 'his own people'.

examples.analysis: *domus ejus* is the household of the woman who is speaking, the subject of *deprecata est*. Classical Latin would have *sua* here; the Vulgate has *ejus*. *meam* in *domum meam* is a regular possessive: accusative singular feminine, agreeing with *domum*, and meaning 'my house', because the speaker is the owner.
